new_statements.translation: Molu p.238: 'Prosody thus captures a single, universal linguistic competence (see Bamba 1991 and Manfredi 1993, whose work seeks to determine at what point prosody reinforces the contrast that distinguishes, for example, French, an accent language, from Bamun, a tone language). The Bamun data indicate a system contrasting two level tones ... high ... and low'; p.276: 'Bamun, which can be defined metrically as an iambic language, first builds a weak foot followed by a strong foot over each metrical domain.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: All opened descriptions treat Bamun/Shupamem as a tone language (Nchare: H, L, LH, HL surface tones with downstep; Molu: two underlying level tones H/B) and give no statement of where word stress falls or whether stress exists. Molu explicitly contrasts Bamun (tone language) with French (accent language); her only prominence claim is a theory-internal metrical one (prefixal domain weak, root domain strong = 'iambic'), used to derive tone melodies rather than to describe audible stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Molu p.276: word-initial syllabic /n/ is assigned a strong metrical node (exception to the weak initial domain) -- a metrical, not a stress, statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Molu's metrical domains are morphological (pre-prefix+prefix domain vs root domain) within the noun; Nchare's tone description covers citation forms and phrasal (downstep across word boundary) contexts. No source discusses phrase-level stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language: Bamun = Shupamem/Shüpamem (bax, bamu1253), Nun subgroup of Eastern Grassfields, spoken around Foumban, Noun division, West Region, Cameroon. Nchare 2012 and Molu 2018 are native-speaker linguists describing the Foumban standard; Ward 1937 worked with speakers at the 1937 Paris Exhibition. Note the tone-inventory disagreement: Nchare posits four tones (H, L, LH, HL), Molu two level tones with derived contours.

sources.locator: Molu 2018 ch.5, p.238 (typology + tone inventory) and p.276 (metrical claim); Nchare 2012 ch.2 p.36 and sec.3.1 p.63
sources.note: No descriptive stress statement. p.238 classes Bamun as 'langue à tons' in contrast to French 'langue à accent', with two level tones H (~225 Hz) and B (~165 Hz); p.276 (and fn. p.110) analyses Bamun within tonal-government/metrical theory as 'métriquement.. une langue iambique' (weak prefixal domain followed by strong root domain) -- a theoretical metrical claim used to derive tone melodies, not an observation about stress.
